items.title: Back-of-envelope: users se requests per second tak ka hisaab
items.one_idea: Turn a user count into requests per second with round numbers and open arithmetic: users x requests per user / 86,400, then multiply by a peak factor.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: रोज़ 10 लाख users हों, तो peak requests per second कैसे निकालोगे?
items.hook_10s: Interviewer ने पूछा: 10 लाख users रोज़, peak requests कितनी? इसका जवाब एक छोटे से हिसाब में है: users से requests, और requests से requests per second। Example से करते हैं। [frame 0: a row of phone icons on the left, an empty server box on the right with a '? req/s' dial]

items.visual_idea: One fixed frame: a row of phone icons feeding a server box. A calculation strip builds left to right in cards (users, x requests, = per day, / 86,400 seconds, = average req/s), then a day-long bar chart gets a tall evening bar that marks the peak, and a final row of small request dots inside the server box shows 'in flight'.
items.everyday_anchor: A railway ticket counter on a festival evening: the day's total tickets sold hides the 6 pm rush the counters must be sized for.
items.example: EXAMPLE (invented, labelled on screen): 10 lakh users, 20 requests per user per day, peak 3x average, 0.2 s per request. 1,000,000 x 20 = 20,000,000 per day; / 86,400 = about 231 average req/s; x 3 = about 700 peak req/s; 700 x 0.2 = about 140 requests in flight (Little's law).
keywords: back of envelope estimation system design
facts_to_verify: Wikipedia (fetched 2026-10-27): QPS is the rate of queries a system gets per second and RPS is the more accurate name for request-response systems; it is used to decide when to scale. The page gives no formula, so the arithmetic is shown on screen, not sourced.
Little's law L = lambda x W (Little's law page): average number in the system = arrival rate x mean time in system; used for the 'in flight' line.
Wikipedia Requests per second: limits depend on operating conditions, no fixed threshold; so the reel gives no per-server capacity number.
All traffic numbers (10 lakh users, 20 requests, 3x peak, 0.2 s) are EXAMPLE; the arithmetic is plain (20,000,000/86,400 = 231.5; x3 = 694; 700 x 0.2 = 140) and needs no source.
No claim about any real company's traffic.
